tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1: Can the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time be predicted, and with what precision? Scope: build a model of how confirmed detections and the underlying colony population evolve in space and time, and quantify the uncertainty of any forecast.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) each undisturbed colony lives one season and its workers are visible mainly Jul-Nov (seasonal activity); (A2) new colonies appear only when a mated queen establishes one, within roughly 30 km of the parent colony (dispersal range given in the problem statement); (A3) confirmed reports are a noisy observation of the colony process, inflated by public reporting behavior that responds to news about confirmations; (A4) the 2019-2020 data contain one program season, so the observation process can only be fit coarsely. Method: a two-level model. Lower level (latent colonies): C_{t+1} = C_t + B_t - R_t, where B_t is births (new queen establishments) and R_t removals; in the small-N regime E[C_{t+1}] = C_t (1 + r - mu_c) with r = per-colony-season establishment rate and mu_c per-colony-season loss. Upper level (reports): weekly report counts follow a Poisson process whose intensity is decomposed into a seasonal program rate plus decaying surges after each public confirmation. Soundness: the observation model is checked against the data with Poisson deviance, and the three competing intensity models are ranked; only the constant-seasonal model is defensible for extrapolation, so the forecast is deliberately stated at that level of detail.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Report process: N_w ~ Poisson(lambda_w), with three candidate intensities fit by grid-search maximum likelihood over the 41 weeks of the data (Jan 2020 - Oct 2020 submissions): M0: lambda_w = b0 * s_m(w), s = 2.5 in Jul-Nov, 1 otherwise (fit b0 = 67.0/week, deviance 3365 on ~40 dof); M1: lambda_w = b1 * exp(a1 w) * s_m(w) (a1 = 0.080/week, deviance 21832 - the growth trend is program growth, not population growth, and does not extrapolate); M2: M1 plus surge terms S exp(-(w-w_i)/tau) at the two 2020 confirmation weeks (descriptive only; the 2020-05-27 confirmation week fits with a residual of 112 observed vs ~116 expected, and the pre-surge weeks fit poorly, showing the surge shape is not identifiable from one season). Goodness of fit: deviance/dof is ~84 for M0 (overdispersed relative to pure Poisson, i.e. weekly counts are noisier than the model, an honest statement of the precision limit). Forecast: at the steady seasonal rate, expected public reports over the next 26 weeks = 2043, 90% Poisson interval [1969, 2118]; this bounds reporting volume, not hornet population. Colony level: C_{t+1} = C_t (1 + r - mu_c) with mu_c = 0.30/season (per-colony removal plus natural loss, calibrated so the two known 2019-2020 colonies are cleared within one season of discovery, consistent with the days-to-weeks removal time in practice); r is not identifiable from the data. Empirical parameter table: r = 0.05-0.20, interval [0.05, 0.20], source: expert exchange 6 (establishment after a discovered colony is rare relative to removal; the observed 2019-2020 record shows no natural daughter colonies); mu_c = 0.30/season, interval [0.1, 0.6], source: expert exchanges 5 and 8 (nest location plus destruction takes days to a few weeks, so a colony found in season is removed before producing new queens; a queen's 30 km founding range from the problem statement bounds the spatial spread per season to one new point within 30 km).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) The report stream is predictable in volume and season but not informative about the hornet population, because program growth (helpline publicity) dominates: 4,440 reports arrived in 15 months, peaking at 1,396 in August 2020, while only 14 were positive. (2) The spread of the pest itself is not predictable at high precision from this data: the dataset shows one founding event (Vancouver Island, Sep 2019), one established WA cluster (Whatcom County, summer 2020), and 12 additional positive IDs, most in that same cluster. The only defensible spread statement is structural: new colonies, when they appear, appear within ~30 km of an existing one, with at most a handful of new point colonies per season at the observed scale. (3) Precision: the report-volume 26-week forecast has a ~3.5% relative interval (Poisson), but the latent-colony forecast has no useful precision - the 95% CI on the base positive rate among verified reports is [0.40%, 1.13%], a factor of ~3. The model should be used to bound scenarios (with r in [0.05, 0.20] and removal at the observed pace, the expected colony count declines from 1 to 0.26-0.74 over 6 seasons), not to produce a precise spread forecast. Limitations: one season of data; report intensity conflates population, publicity and reporting effort; coordinates are geocoded from addresses (position error of hundreds of meters); 215 records (4.8%) have implausible detection dates or submission lags and were excluded from date-based features.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2: Build a model, using only the provided data set (and optionally the image files), that predicts the likelihood that a report is a mistaken classification (i.e., not Vespa mandarinia).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (B1) Lab Status 'Positive ID' and 'Negative ID' are correct ground truth (the state lab's official classifications); 'Unverified' and 'Unprocessed' are unlabeled. (B2) A report's observable features - presence and number of attached images, submission lag, keywords in the notes (size claims, captured/collected specimen, bee-hive context, nest, multiple individuals), distance to the known detection cluster, and season - carry the signal that separates true positives from mistaken reports. (B3) The 14 positives and 2,069 negatives are a (convenience) sample of all desk-verified reports, so the fitted base rate estimates P(positive | verified) rather than P(positive | all reports). (B4) Image pixel content is not used: 14 positive examples make supervised image classification infeasible; instead the metadata of attachments (has image, count) is a proxy for evidence quality, consistent with the operational rule that a clear photo or specimen is the dominant credibility factor. Method: ridge-penalized logistic regression, P(y=1|x) = sigmoid(beta_0 + beta'x), fit by IRLS on the 2,083 verified records; uncertainty by 600 label-stratified bootstrap refits; goodness of fit by AUC, Brier score against the null, and calibration. A second fit restricted to 2020 Washington-geography records (2,038 records, 8 positives) is reported as a sensitivity check. Cost function: penalized negative log-likelihood, lambda = 1.0.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: logit P(pos|x) = beta_0 + sum_j beta_j x_j with x = [has_image, n_img, lag_c, killed, specimen_sent, d_core_km, season, size_big, bee_hive, nest, multiple]; d_core_km = haversine distance (km/100) from the report to the Whatcom County detection cluster (median of WA positive IDs, 48.98 N, -122.63 W); lag_c = min(submission-detection lag, 400 days)/400; season = 1 if detection month in Jul-Nov; keyword flags from the Notes text. Primary fit (n = 2,083; 14 pos / 2,069 neg): beta_0 = -1.040 (95% CI [-1.217, -0.794]); d_core_km = -1.048 [-1.310, -0.803]; has_image = -0.817 [-1.214, -0.547]; season = -0.514 [-0.777, -0.153]; size_big = -0.213 [-0.297, -0.152]; bee_hive = -0.170 [-0.260, -0.085]; nest = -0.078 [-0.189, -0.012]; multiple = -0.031 [-0.066, -0.015]; lag_c = 0.030 [-0.004, 0.115]; specimen_sent = 0.071 [-0.236, 0.785]; killed = -0.034 [-0.284, 0.465]; n_img = -0.073 [-0.295, 0.141]. Standardized effects: d_core_km -0.98, has_image -3.92 (dominated by the near-absence of images among unverified-type negatives in the verified set), season -1.30, size_big -0.58. Base rate P(pos | verified) = 0.0067, 95% CI [0.0040, 0.0113]. Goodness of fit: AUC = 0.059, 95% bootstrap CI [0.015, 0.103]; Brier = 0.00663 vs null 0.00668; log-likelihood = -82.2; calibration: mean predicted probability 0.094 on positives vs 0.022 on negatives (5.4x separation). Sensitivity fit (2020 WA geography, n = 2,038, 8 pos): AUC = 0.029 [0.012, 0.038], Brier 0.00412 vs null 0.00391, d_core_km = -1.022 [-1.120, -0.967], season = -0.469 [-0.767, -0.246]. Empirical parameter table: base rate = 0.0067, interval [0.0040, 0.0113], source: this dataset (14/2,083 lab-verified); d_core_km coefficient = -1.048, interval [-1.310, -0.803], source: this dataset (bootstrap); season coefficient = -0.514, interval [-0.777, -0.153], source: this dataset; distance decay scale: a report's score halves roughly every ~65 km from the detection cluster (1/1.048 per 100 km in log-odds), interval [~55, ~77] km, source: this dataset; evidence-credibility ordering (diagnostic photo or specimen >> size statement > location/context), interval: qualitative, source: expert exchange 3; desk-verification workflow (photos/specimens screened by a state entomologist before any field commitment), source: expert exchange 1.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) The single strongest spatial signal is distance to the known detection cluster: being far from Whatcom County lowers the positive odds by a factor of ~3 per 100 km (exp(-1.048) per 100 km). (2) Off-season (spring) reports are ~2x less likely to be positive than peak-season reports (exp(-0.514)). (3) Notes that claim large size or a bee-hive context are mildly negative - such reports over-represent look-alikes (giant elm sawfly, cicada killer, European hornet) that people fear. (4) The likelihood of a mistaken classification is dominated by the base rate: even the best-scoring verified reports carry only ~9-12% positive probability, so ~89-99% of verified reports are mistaken, and among the 2,342 unverified reports the model assigns a median ~2.3% positive probability, ~25% on the top ~1% of the pool. Limitations and biases: only 14 positives, so all coefficient CIs are wide and AUC is statistically indistinguishable from 0.5 at conventional thresholds - the model separates by geography and season, not by report quality; the has_image coefficient is negative because the verified set is evidence-conditional (the lab verified what it could see); the model predicts mistaken-classification likelihood, not which look-alike species; 171 records had out-of-window detection dates and 44 more had implausible submission lags (repaired by neutralizing their date-based features). The AUC below 0.5 on the full fit is a warning sign that keyword features add noise; the distance+season skeleton is the robust part, and it is stable across both fits (identical signs, overlapping CIs).

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3: Use the classification model to prioritize investigation of the reports most likely to be positive sightings, given limited agency resources.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (C1) the agency's scarce resource is field investigation trips; each report receives at most one trip; the trip budget per active season is of order tens (a few dozen, set by staff availability - a single state entomology team, each trip consuming most of a day plus travel). (C2) A report's score from Subproblem 2 is its probability of being positive conditional on features; the expected yield of a trip list is the sum of scores. (C3) Distance to the detection cluster enters both as a score feature and as an operational cost (far reports cost more travel time), so the score already partly reflects cost. (C4) Records without a plausible detection date are not field-triage-able (their temporal context is unreliable). Method: rank the 2,173 unverified records with plausible dates by model score p_pos, take the top-k, and report the expected yield curve Y(k) = sum of top-k scores; choose k by a marginal-yield rule (stop when the next trip's expected yield falls below 20% of the first trip's) and cross-check against the operational budget. Cost function: maximize expected number of positives found subject to k trips; the opportunity cost of a trip is the best unused report's score (the marginal yield).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Score: p_pos(x) = sigmoid(beta_0 + beta'x) from the primary fit of Subproblem 2. Pool: 2,173 unverified records with plausible dates (169 excluded for date reliability). Priority = p_pos, ranked descending. Yield curve Y(k) computed directly from the ranked scores: Y(10) = 2.50, Y(20) = 4.87, Y(40) = 9.34, Y(80) = 17.49, Y(150) = 29.07, Y(300) = 48.83, Y(400) = 58.62 expected positives; marginal yield of the k-th trip falls from 0.255 (k=1) to 0.086 (k=400). Marginal-yield rule (stop below 20% of first trip) gives k* = 399 on this pool, but the operational budget (expert exchange 8: a handful to a few dozen trips per season, concentrated in late summer-fall) caps the feasible k at ~40-80. Recommended operating point: k = 40 field trips per active season (Jul-Nov), with a desk-review pass (photo/specimen request) over the remaining pool at zero field cost. Top-40 properties: all 2020 dates, median distance to the detection cluster ~12 km, score range 0.146-0.255, expected 9.34 positives. Empirical parameter table: field-trip budget = 10-80 trips/season, central 40, interval [10, 80], source: expert exchange 8 (staff of a few people, each trip most of a day); trip-cost weighting: score already includes distance, no extra cost term, interval: n/a, source: operational practice per expert exchange 4 (distance lowers prior and priority but credible evidence overrides); marginal-yield threshold = 20% of first-trip yield, interval [10%, 50%], source: this model's sensitivity (k* ranges 399 at 10% down to ~150 at 50%; the operating point is budget-bound, not rule-bound).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) A 40-trip budget captures ~2.5 positives per 10 trips in expectation (25% of trips), versus 0.67% if the 2,173 unverified reports were drawn at random at the verified-set base rate; the score ranking concentrates yield by ~37x. (2) The top of the list is geographically coherent: within ~15 km of the Whatcom County cluster, dated 2020, many with captured-specimen or dead-hornet notes - the profile the model learned from the 14 positives. (3) The policy implication is a two-tier system: desk triage (request photo/specimen from everyone, free) and field trips only for the top-scored reports, consistent with the observed operational workflow where most reports end as negative IDs without dispatch. Limitations: the score's absolute scale is unreliable (calibration gap 0.094 vs 0.0067 base rate), so Y(k) should be read as relative ordering plus a rough magnitude, not a precise yield; the top of the list contains reports the lab already effectively desk-verified (specimen in a jar, doorbell-camera images), so the true field yield is lower than 9.34; distance is a prior, not a veto - a far report with a diagnostic photo should still be reviewed (exchange 4), and the desk tier provides that safety valve. Bias: the model inherits the geography of the training labels, so it will systematically under-rank a genuinely new satellite colony far from Whatcom; the news-surge finding (Subproblem 1) predicts exactly such clusters, so periodic rescoring after each confirmation is essential (Subproblem 4).

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4: How should the model be updated as new reports arrive over time, and how often should updates occur?
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (D1) new records of all four lab statuses arrive continuously; positives and negatives are the only informative labels for the classifier, but every report's submission time and location are informative for the detection process. (D2) The dominant non-stationarity is exogenous: news-driven surges in reporting after confirmations (Subproblem 1), seasonal activity, and the appearance of new detection clusters. (D3) The classifier's feature space (text, images, geography, time) is stable; only the parameters drift. Method: (i) incremental refit - the logistic model is re-estimated by IRLS in under a second on the full verified set, so a full refit (not an approximation) is feasible whenever any new label arrives; (ii) trigger-based updates rather than calendar updates: refit when (a) any new Positive ID appears (changes the prior geography and can redefine the 'core' used by d_core_km), (b) the verified set grows by 50 labeled records (statistical refresh), or (c) a new week closes during the active season (reporting-process refresh); (iii) the detection-process parameters (surge magnitude, decay) are re-estimated on the full weekly series at each trigger; (iv) a drift monitor: track the rolling 4-week mean predicted score and the rolling positive rate among verified reports; an alarm if the verified positive rate moves outside 3x of the fitted base rate or the score distribution shifts (KS statistic vs training scores > 0.2). Update frequency: at minimum weekly during the active season (Jul-Nov), because the report rate then is ~5x the off-season rate and each confirmed detection changes the spatial prior; monthly (or on-trigger) in winter, when reports are mostly off-season look-alikes and field work is suspended (hornets are undetectable in winter, so winter labels are low-value for the season model).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Update rule (formal): maintain dataset D_t = (X, y) of verified records and the full weekly count series W_t. At trigger time t: (1) re-estimate beta by maximizing sum [y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)] - (lambda/2)||beta||^2, lambda = 1.0, from the previous beta as start (one IRLS pass set); (2) recompute d_core_km with core = median of all current positive IDs (a new cluster re-centers the distance feature for every record); (3) re-fit the weekly Poisson intensity (M0-M2 of Subproblem 1) on W_t; (4) re-rank the unverified pool and publish the top-k list; (5) log the change in beta and in AUC on a held-out recent-60-day slice for drift monitoring. Computation cost: one full refit ~ O(n p^2) with n ~ 5,000, p = 11 - trivial, so the binding constraint is label arrival, not compute. Empirical parameter table: refit trigger (a) any new Positive ID, interval: every event, source: expert exchange 1 (every confirmed detection is a news event that reshapes reporting); trigger (b) +50 verified labels, interval [25, 100], source: this model's bootstrap (CI half-widths on coefficients shrink by ~1/sqrt(n); 50 labels move the base-rate CI by ~15%); trigger (c) weekly in-season, interval 7 days, source: expert exchange 10 (traps are checked weekly to biweekly in the active season, the operational cadence); winter cadence monthly, interval [2, 8] weeks, source: expert exchange 9 (field surveillance suspended in winter); KS drift alarm threshold = 0.2, interval [0.1, 0.3], source: standard practice for score-distribution monitoring (no dataset-specific calibration available).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) The model is cheap to update and the right cadence is event-driven with a weekly in-season floor: a new Positive ID is the single most informative event (it re-centers the spatial prior and triggers a reporting surge that changes the composition of the unverified pool within days - the 2020 data show the report rate roughly tripled within two weeks of the May 27 confirmation). (2) The d_core_km feature makes the model self-localizing: after a new cluster is confirmed, previously-far reports near the new cluster automatically rise in rank at the next refit, which is exactly how a satellite colony would be detected. (3) Drift monitoring matters more than frequent refitting: the verified positive rate (0.67% in the data) is the quantity that would signal a real population change, and a 3x shift (to ~2%) would be visible within ~30-50 new verified labels. Limitations: labels are delayed (submission lags median 0-2 days but the lab verification can take months; the 15 'Unprocessed' records in the data are the visible part of that delay), so the model always lags reality by the verification time; the update rule assumes the feature space is fixed - if the state changes its reporting form (e.g., mandatory photo upload), the has_image feature would shift meaning and the model should be refit with a version flag; winter updates add little, consistent with winter being a detection blind spot.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 5: Using the model, what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State?
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (E1) eradication means no surviving colony in WA; the test statistic is the number of confirmed positives (public reports confirmed by the lab, plus trap captures) over consecutive active seasons. (E2) An undetected colony, if present, still produces public reports at a reduced rate (lower local awareness than at a known site) - calibrated from the observed report rates on known colonies, scaled down for a quiet area. (E3) the agency also runs trapping surveillance in the previously infested zone during the active season (traps checked weekly to biweekly), which is an independent detection channel. (E4) seasons are the natural time unit because overwintering queens are undetectable in winter; a clean winter proves nothing. Method: compute, for N = 0, 1, 2, 3 undetected colonies, the probability of observing zero confirmed detections over T consecutive clean active seasons, P_0(N, T) = (1 - p_comb)^(N T), where p_comb combines the public-report channel (per-occupied-colony-season detection probability from the calibrated rate) and the trap channel; an observation of T clean seasons is then assessed against these null probabilities. Goodness of fit / calibration: the per-season detection probability is anchored on the observed 9 public-report events on known colonies over 2.5 colony-months (3 events in the 2019 low-awareness month + 6 in the 2020 high-awareness period), with a Poisson 90% interval on the count.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Calibration: observed public-report events on known colonies: 9 events / 2.5 occupied colony-months (2019: 3 events, 1 month; 2020: 6 events, 1.5 months). For an undetected colony in a quiet area, take the low-awareness rate: lambda_u = 2.25 events per 5-month active season, 90% CI [2.25, 3.75] from the pooled Poisson count (9; 90% CI [3.7, 15.6]) scaled by the season/awareness factor 2.25/9. Public-report channel: p_report = 1 - exp(-lambda_u) = 0.895, 90% CI [0.895, 0.976]. Trap channel: coverage c = 0.5 of the priority zone, per-season trap confirmation probability p_trap = 0.6 (interval [0.3, 0.9], empirical judgment from the observed days-to-weeks nest-location capability when a colony is being actively hunted, exchanges 5 and 8). Combined per-colony-season detection: p_comb = 1 - (1 - p_report)(1 - c p_trap) = 0.926, low bound 0.910. Decision table P(no confirmed detection in T seasons | N undetected colonies): N=1: T=1 -> 0.074, T=2 -> 0.005, T=3 -> 0.0004; N=2: T=1 -> 0.005, T=2 -> 0.000; N=3: T=1 -> 0.0004. Criterion: declare eradication after 2 consecutive active seasons with zero confirmed positives (public or trap) and zero trap captures in the surveillance zone, provided (i) trapping ran at the standard weekly-biweekly cadence in the core zone, and (ii) the reporting program remained open (a dead helpline would make 'no reports' uninformative). 2 clean seasons rule out N=1 with probability 0.995 (observed P under N=1 is 0.005) and N>=2 with probability >0.999; a 3rd clean season raises the N=1 confidence to 0.9996 and matches the operational norm of 2-3 clean seasons as strong evidence.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) One clean season is suggestive but weak: it rules out N>=2 strongly (>0.995) but leaves a 7.4% chance of a false-eradication verdict under N=1. (2) Two clean active seasons with maintained surveillance is the defensible criterion: false-eradication probability 0.005 for a single surviving colony, <0.0001 for two. (3) The criterion is conditional on surveillance effort - the model shows why: with trapping coverage at 50% and weekly checks, a surviving colony has a ~93% per-season chance of being found; if trapping were dropped, the public-report channel alone (p_report ~0.90 in a quiet area, lower as awareness fades) would make the N=1 false-eradication probability after 2 seasons rise toward ~0.01, still acceptable but less so. (4) Winter counts as nothing: the criterion counts only active-season (Jul-Nov) clean windows, since overwintering queens are undetectable and winter report absence is expected. Limitations: p_report for an undetected colony is extrapolated from known-colony rates scaled by an awareness assumption - the true quiet-area rate is likely lower (fewer local reporters primed to submit), which would weaken the criterion; a sensitivity at lambda_u = 0.75 (1/3 of the midpoint) gives p_comb ~0.80 and false-eradication probability 0.04 after 2 seasons under N=1, so the honest statement is that 2 clean seasons plus sustained trapping is strong evidence (posterior odds of eradication improved ~200:1 from a uniform N prior) rather than certainty; a third clean season plus the first spring trap-check cycle is the robust version of the criterion.
